metadata.note: The Western Vermont Railroad's main line, North Bennington - Arlington - Manchester - Danby - Wallingford - Rutland, and its successors. This is the line the short state line-to-North Bennington branch in troy_boston_hoosick_bennington.geojson was built to feed: together they gave Rutland a route west to Troy over the Troy & Bennington and Troy & Boston. A third feature is the 1854 branch that finally brought the rails into Bennington village itself, which the main line missed by five miles: north of Bennington it is still active Vermont Railway freight track, south of there an abandoned right-of-way running down to the old depot on Depot Street. The two main-line features share the same geometry, one per era of ownership - the independent Western Vermont (1852-1865) and the Bennington & Rutland / Rutland Railroad that grew out of it (1865-1953) - following the same one-feature-per-company-era pattern as cities/albany_commuter_rail.geojson. Geometry is the real track centerline from OpenStreetMap, routed over the still-active Vermont Railway B&R Main Line and B&R Subdivision, which is the original alignment; it measures 52 miles North Bennington-Rutland against the 55 miles usually quoted for Bennington-Rutland, the difference being the five miles from Bennington up to North Bennington. Era boundaries follow real, sourced corporate milestones; headway_min and avg_speed_kmh are estimates, not real timetables.
sources: https://www.rutlandrailroad.org/history/timeline/ (Rutland Railroad Historical Society timeline: Western Vermont Railroad incorporated November 5 1845; leased to the Troy & Boston November 1 1857; first Bennington & Rutland Railroad Company formed from the Western Vermont August 1 1865; Troy & Boston lease terminated January 15-16 1868 and the line leased by John Page and J. Gregory Smith; Bennington & Rutland and Lebanon Springs consolidated into the Harlem Extension R.R. in January 1870; Vermont Central terminates its lease of the Bennington & Rutland in 1877; third Rutland Railroad Company formed by consolidation with the Bennington & Rutland September 6 1901; passenger service terminated on the Chatham Division June 25 1932; ICC approves Chatham branch abandonment May 20 1953)

https://bennington.pastperfectonline.com/bysearchterm?keyword=Western+Vermont+Railroad (Bennington Museum: Western Vermont Railroad completed 1852 between North Bennington and Rutland, later became the Bennington & Rutland Railroad; the 55-mile line was open for service by May 1852)

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bennington_station (Bennington's early rail service was limited to North Bennington about five miles north of downtown; the Bennington & Rutland ran a branch from North Bennington into the town center in 1854)

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bennington_station (in 1854 a branch was extended from North Bennington, about five miles north, to serve downtown Bennington, with a wood frame depot erected at the time; the present stone station was built 1897-98 to a design by local architect William C. Bull and is the only Richardsonian Romanesque railroad station in Vermont; passenger service to downtown Bennington ended in the early 1930s; the building was sold into private hands in 1966, became a restaurant in 1970 that closed in 2018, and was listed on the National Register of Historic Places November 9 1988)

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rutland_Railroad (a three-week employee strike in 1953 permanently ended Rutland passenger service, taking the Green Mountain Flyer and Mount Royal with it; after further labor trouble the Rutland applied in early 1961 to abandon its entire system, approval was granted and operations ceased later that year; the State of Vermont bought substantial portions in 1963 and they are now operated by the Vermont Railway)

https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Bennington_station (Lebanon Springs Railroad built 1869 south from Bennington to Chatham NY, acquired by the Rutland in 1899; Second Empire station built 1880; freight resumed in 1964 under the Vermont Railway)
metadata.not_yet_sourced: Frequency for every era is estimated. The exact day in May 1852 the through line opened, and the precise 1953 date the last passenger train ran, are not pinned down. The exact date passenger service ended on the Bennington village branch is not sourced beyond 'the early 1930s'; 1932 is used here. Wikipedia credits the 1854 branch to the Bennington & Rutland, but that name did not exist until August 1 1865, so it is attributed to the Western Vermont here. Sources disagree on when the Bennington & Rutland became part of the Rutland: the North Bennington station article says merged in 1867, while the Rutland Railroad Historical Society timeline dates the formal consolidation to September 6 1901 and shows a run of leases in between - the timeline is followed here.
metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.

segments.note: Incorporated November 5 1845, the Western Vermont had its 55-mile line open for service by May 1852, running north out of North Bennington through Shaftsbury, Arlington, Sunderland, Manchester, East Dorset, Danby, Wallingford and Clarendon to Rutland. Bennington village itself sat five miles off the line and did not get its own branch from North Bennington until 1854. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable

segments.note: The main line to Rutland ran through North Bennington and missed Bennington village by five miles, so in 1854 a branch was run down from North Bennington into the town center and a wood frame depot put up there. Wikipedia credits the branch to the Bennington & Rutland, but the company did not take that name until 1865 - in 1854 it was still the Western Vermont. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable
sources: Segment-level: this segment's own note carries the citation for its dates and service. Supporting references for the line:

segments.note: Under the Bennington & Rutland from August 1 1865. The branch's job never changed: shuttle Bennington's passengers and freight the five miles up to North Bennington, where the Rutland line, the Chatham line and the Troy branch all met. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable
sources: Segment-level: this segment's own note carries the citation for its dates and service. Supporting references for the line:

segments.note: The wooden depot had run down by the 1890s and was replaced in 1897-98 by the stone station on Depot Street, designed by local architect William C. Bull - the only Richardsonian Romanesque railroad station in Vermont. Passenger service into downtown Bennington ended in the early 1930s, replaced by buses. The depot was sold in 1966, was a restaurant from 1970 until 2018, holds offices now, and has been on the National Register of Historic Places since November 9 1988; the northern half of the branch is still Vermont Railway freight track. estimated; frequency not sourced from a real timetable
